speeches.speaker: Mark Dreyfus
speeches.brief: Presented consequential amendments supporting the Public Interest Disclosure Bill 2013, Australia's first federal whistleblower protection scheme, giving the Commonwealth Ombudsman and the Inspector-General of Intelligence and Security oversight of how agencies handle public interest disclosures.

speeches.speaker: Melissa Parke
speeches.brief: Supported the Public Interest Disclosure Bill 2013, Australia's first stand-alone federal whistleblower protection scheme, praising Attorney-General Mark Dreyfus for chairing the 2008 parliamentary inquiry that led to it, and said the legislation supports Australia's compliance with the United Nations Convention against Corruption.

speeches.speaker: Daryl Melham
speeches.brief: Supported the Public Interest Disclosure Bill, quoting a Parliamentary Library research paper noting the Commonwealth was the only Australian jurisdiction without dedicated legislation protecting whistleblowers, after a series of earlier private members' bills had lapsed for lack of government support.

speeches.speaker: Daryl Melham
speeches.brief: Supported the Public Interest Disclosure Bill, which stems from a February 2009 parliamentary committee report, but warned against frivolous complaints modelled on experience with the New South Wales ICAC process, which can damage reputations before allegations are substantiated, and said the legislation would need tweaking over time.

speeches.speaker: Mark Dreyfus
speeches.brief: Summed up the second reading debate on the Public Interest Disclosure Bill, noting House and Senate committees had together received more than 30 submissions and both recommended the bill pass, and confirmed the scheme covers intelligence agencies internally while excluding members of parliament, their staff and federal judicial officers from its protections.

speeches.speaker: Mark Dreyfus
speeches.brief: Argued that neither proposed amendment to the Public Interest Disclosure (Consequential Amendments) Bill 2013 was necessary or desirable, saying the first could disrupt responsibilities among the Ombudsman, Public Service Commissioner and Parliamentary Service Commissioner, while the second was covered by the Ombudsman's existing jurisdiction.
